scenes.narration: The internet says wolves reshaped Yellowstone, even changing the course of its rivers. The data says: it's only half true.
scenes.title: THE WOLF EFFECT

scenes.narration: Gone by 1926, wolves came from Canada: 14 in 1995, 17 in 1996.
scenes.label: NORTHERN RANGE
scenes.caption: 31 WOLVES

scenes.narration: Elk fell from 19,045 in 1994 to 3,915 in 2013, down 79 percent.
Ecologists call this a trophic cascade: predators thin herbivores, and plants recover. Where browsing eased, willows grew taller, and beavers gained food and building material.
Beaver colonies did rise, from one in 1996 to twelve by 2009.
The viral story ends at rivers, but that is where the evidence thins.
Willows grew taller but covered no more ground, and incised streams limit recovery. Hunting, drought and grizzlies also cut elk numbers, so wolves were not alone.
scenes.caption: HALF TRUE

scenes.narration: In 2025, 6,124 of 7,226 counted elk were outside the park's protection.
scenes.caption: 85% OUTSIDE

scenes.narration: Wolves mattered, but the cascade was patchier and weaker than the legend says. Follow for more.

sources.claim: 14 wolves captured in Canada (Alberta) and released 1995; 17 more captured in Canada (British Columbia) in 1996; 10-week acclimation pens (NPS Yellowstone Wolf Project Biennial Report 1995-1996)
41 wolves released in total, 1995-1997: 14 from Alberta, 17 from British Columbia, 10 from northwest Montana (NPS, Yellowstone Science 24-1)
Yellowstone's last wolf pack was killed in 1926; wolves were absent as a breeding population until 1995 (NPS History of Wolf Management; an NPS finding aid dates the last known den destroyed to 1923)
Wolf population peak: at least 174 wolves at end of 2003 (NPS 2003 annual wolf report)
124 wolves in 11 packs at end of 2023 (NPS 2023 wolf report)
108 wolves in 9 packs at end of 2024; April-2024 helicopter count of 5,597 northern-herd elk (NPS 2024 wolf/cougar/elk report)

84 wolves in 7 packs at end of 2025; April-2025 helicopter count of 7,226 northern-herd elk, 6,124 outside the park (Montana) and 1,102 inside; counts are minimum estimates (NPS 2025 wolf/cougar/elk report)
Yellowstone wolf population declined in 2025 (84 at year end), corroborating the NPS 2025 report

Record-high 19,045 northern-range elk counted in January 1994; 3,915 in 2013, only 743 above the 1968 low; December 1994 count already 2,254 lower than the year before (NPS Yellowstone Science 24-1). Decline 19,045 -> 3,915 = -79.4%
Same NPS article: scientific consensus on the role of wolves in northern-herd dynamics has not yet emerged; modern aerial counts underestimate true abundance (Yellowstone Science 24(1), 2016)
December 2002 northern-herd count of 9,215 elk (Northern Yellowstone Cooperative Wildlife Working Group, via Bozeman Daily Chronicle)

December 2010 count of 4,635 elk, down 24% from 6,070 the previous year; drought, grizzly predation (bears ~58% of calf deaths May-Sept), wolf predation, and Gardiner late-hunt permits cut from 1,102 (2005) to 100 (2006-10) and eliminated in 2011; Doug Smith: wolves are not the only reason; northern-range wolves 94 (2007) -> 37 (2010)
March 2019 count of about 5,800 elk, 23% below 2018's 7,579; 7,510 in 2016; 10-year average 5,399 (Montana FWP / Working Group)

Trophic cascade definition; willow/aspen height has increased in existing stands but not in area, possibly dependent on beaver occupation; ongoing scientific debate (NPS, The Big Scientific Debate: Trophic Cascades)

Beaver colonies in the study area rose from 1 in 1996 to 12 in 2009; trees and shrubs recovering along some streams (Oregon State University Trophic Cascades Program, Ripple & Beschta; press release Dec 2011)

Willow recovery limited by stream down-cutting and water availability, not browsing alone: plots with beaver dams plus fences grew >500 cm vs ~60 cm in controls over 17 years (Cooper, Hobbs et al., ESA 2017 abstract)
Sampling only the tallest young aspen overstated regeneration 3-8x versus random sampling; random sampling still showed a cascade but a weaker one (Brice, Larsen & MacNulty 2022, Ecology Letters)
Viral 'wolves change rivers' claim and its scientific scrutiny (International Wolf Center, 'Do wolves really change rivers?')
